newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Dutch hit EU over "double standards" on rights.
newsitem.headline: Dutch hit EU over "double standards" on rights.

text.p: The Netherlands, holder of the rotating European Union presidency, has suggested key member countries are applying double standards on human rights, according to a letter circulated in Geneva on Friday.

The letter, from Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo to his EU colleagues, was sparked by a French refusal to back a joint resolution condemning China at the United Nations Human Rights Commission which is currently in session.

"To my great regret, one partner has informed the presidency that his country is not prepared to participate in the tabling of a human rights resolution on China," said the letter, which did not mention France directly.

Copies of the letter, which Dutch officials confirmed was authentic, were circulating among delegates to the 53-member Human Rights Commission, which for the past six years has rebuffed EU-U.S. efforts to censure China.

Van Mierlo said he now understood that three other EU countries -- said by diplomats to be Germany, Spain and Italy -- had taken up the same position as France, which declared last week that dialogue with China was better than confrontation.
As current president, the Netherlands was expected to present the annual EU-sponsored resolution -- with strong backing from the United States -- on behalf of all 15 members.

But van Mierlo said the position taken by the four was not only a serious setback for prospects of a common EU foreign policy but much worse put at stake "the essence of the human rights policy of the Union."

In earlier discussions he had "qualified as the core of our policy that obviously none of us wants to apply a double standard with regard to the human rights situation in the world: one for powerful countries, one for smaller ones," he added.
Van Mierlo said while a degree of differentiation within the EU might be possible where concrete measures were concerned -- "with United Nations resolutions it is inconceivable."

The "change of policy" on China represented by the stance of the four -- of whom only France has declared its position publicly -- directly affected the Union's credibility in sponsoring other resolutions at the Commission, he added.
As a result, the EU as a Union "should refrain from any initiative to obtain comparable condemnations of other countries where human rights are being violated," he said.

Dutch officials said EU motions this year must be tabled by the Netherlands as president. Diplomats said France challenged this and would take it up at a Sunday meeting of EU foreign ministers in the Hague.

The Dutch move appeared to block four draft EU motions condemning Burma, Iran, Iraq and Zaire at the Commission -- itself long criticised by human rights groups for the politicisation of its debates and the selective nature of its resolutions.

China itself has accused the West of using the body to attack developing countries, which have an overall majority in the Commission. Rights groups say the big powers work hard backstage to ensure allies do not come under full scrutiny.

Western efforts to have a resolution passed on Beijing's rights performance have failed every year since 1990, as China has rallied enough support each time for a vote in the Commission of "no action."

U.S. ambassador to the United Nations in New York, Bill Richardson, told reporters in Geneva this week that Washington wanted to see a resolution condemning China this year, but preferred the Europeans take the lead.
He said he would be campaigning in Geneva against a "no acation" motion. But he declined to say whether Washington would draft and table a resolution if the EU dropped its annual bid.
